```{r, include=FALSE}
library(highcharter)
hc_set_theme("hcrt", tooltip = list(valueDecimals = 2))
```

Explore complete charts and expand **Show R code** below each one to see how it was built.
For short examples grouped by data shape, see [Chart types](chart-types.html).

## HIMYM example

> This is a bar graph describing my favorite pies including a pie chart describing my favorite bars.
> - _Marshall Eriksen_

<style>
.himym-chart .highchart { height: auto !important; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; min-height: 300px; }
</style>

::: {.himym-chart}

```{r bar, echo=FALSE}
favorite_bars <- data.frame(
  bar = c(
    "Mclaren's",
    "McGee's",
    "P & G",
    "White Horse Tavern",
    "King Cole Bar"
  ),
  percent = c(30, 28, 27, 12, 3)
)
favorite_pies <- data.frame(
  pie = c(
    "Strawberry Rhubarb",
    "Pumpkin",
    "Lemon Meringue",
    "Blueberry",
    "Key Lime"
  ),
  percent = c(85, 64, 75, 100, 57)
)

highchart() |>
  # Data
  hc_add_series(
    favorite_pies,
    "column",
    hcaes(
      x = pie,
      y = percent
    ),
    name = "Pie"
  ) |>
  hc_add_series(
    favorite_bars,
    "pie",
    hcaes(
      name = bar,
      y = percent
    ),
    name = "Bars"
  ) |>
  # Options for each type of series
  hc_plotOptions(
    series = list(
      showInLegend = FALSE,
      pointFormat = "{point.y}%",
      colorByPoint = TRUE
    ),
    pie = list(
      center = c("83%", "46%"),
      size = "62%",
      dataLabels = list(enabled = FALSE)
    )
  ) |>
  # Axis
  hc_yAxis(
    width = "64%",
    title = list(text = "percentage of tastiness"),
    labels = list(format = "{value}%"),
    max = 100
  ) |>
  hc_xAxis(
    width = "64%",
    categories = favorite_pies$pie
  ) |>
  # Titles, subtitle, caption and credits
  hc_title(
    text = "How I Met Your Mother: Pie Chart Bar Graph"
  ) |>
  hc_subtitle(
    text = "This is a bar graph describing my favorite pies
    including a pie chart describing my favorite bars"
  ) |>
  hc_caption(
    text = "The values represented are in percentage of tastiness and awesomeness."
  ) |>
  hc_credits(
    enabled = TRUE,
    text = "Source: HIMYM",
    href = "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f_J8QU1m0Ng",
    style = list(fontSize = "12px")
  )
```

:::

## Charts inside tooltips

These two Gapminder examples come from [Using tooltips in unexpected ways](https://jkunst.com/blog/posts/2019-02-04-using-tooltips-in-unexpected-ways/).

### A country's population over time

Each bubble is a country in 2007. Hover over one to see its population from 1952 to 2007.
The `ttdata` column holds that country's observations as a list of points.

```{r tooltip-gapminder, echo=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(highcharter)

gp <- gapminder::gapminder |>
  arrange(desc(year)) |>
  distinct(country, .keep_all = TRUE)
```

```{r tooltip-population, echo=FALSE}
gp2 <- gapminder::gapminder |>
  select(country, x = year, y = pop) |>
  group_nest(country, .key = "ttdata") |>
  mutate(ttdata = map(ttdata, list_parse))

gptot <- left_join(gp, gp2, by = "country")

hchart(
  gptot,
  "point",
  hcaes(lifeExp, gdpPercap, name = country, size = pop, group = continent)
) |>
  hc_yAxis(type = "logarithmic") |>
  hc_tooltip(
    useHTML = TRUE,
    headerFormat = "<b>{point.key}</b>",
    pointFormatter = tooltip_chart(
      accesor = "ttdata",
      hc_opts = list(
        series = list(list(name = "point.name")),
        tooltip = list(
          headerFormat = "{point.x}<br>",
          pointFormat = "{series.name}: {point.y:,.0f}"
        )
      )
    )
  )
```

### A scatter plot inside a donut

Each slice represents a continent's share of the 2007 population. Hover over a
slice to see its countries in the center of the donut. The scatter plot shows
life expectancy on the horizontal axis and GDP per capita on the vertical axis.

```{r tooltip-donut, echo=FALSE}
donutdata <- gp |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(pop = sum(as.double(pop)), .groups = "drop")

donutdata2 <- gp |>
  select(continent, name = country, x = lifeExp, y = gdpPercap) |>
  group_nest(continent, .key = "ttdata") |>
  mutate(ttdata = map(ttdata, list_parse)) |>
  left_join(donutdata, by = "continent")

hchart(
  donutdata2,
  "pie",
  hcaes(name = continent, y = pop),
  name = "Population share",
  innerSize = "78%"
) |>
  hc_tooltip(
    useHTML = TRUE,
    headerFormat = "<b>{point.key}</b>",
    pointFormatter = tooltip_chart(
      accesor = "ttdata",
      hc_opts = list(
        chart = list(type = "scatter"),
        series = list(list(name = "point.name")),
        tooltip = list(
          headerFormat = "<b>{point.name}</b><br>",
          pointFormat = "Life expectancy: {point.x:.1f} years<br>GDP per capita: ${point.y:,.0f}"
        ),
        credits = list(enabled = FALSE),
        plotOptions = list(scatter = list(marker = list(radius = 2)))
      ),
      width = 200,
      height = 150
    ),
    positioner = JS(
      "function (width, height) {
      const chart = this.chart, center = chart.series[0].center;
      return {
        x: chart.plotLeft + center[0] - width / 2,
        y: chart.plotTop + center[1] - height / 2
      };
    }"
    ),
    shadow = FALSE,
    borderWidth = 0,
    backgroundColor = "transparent",
    hideDelay = 1000
  )
```

## A reading survey on a Likert scale

Where do readers agree, and where are they divided? Each row in this
illustrative survey adds to 100%. The midpoint of the neutral response sits
at zero. Click **Neutral** in the legend to toggle both halves together.

```{r reading-survey, echo=FALSE}
survey <- data.frame(
  item = c("I read for pleasure", "I discuss books", "I prefer print"),
  strongly_disagree = c(5, 12, 15),
  disagree = c(10, 28, 20),
  neutral = c(15, 20, 30),
  agree = c(40, 30, 20),
  strongly_agree = c(30, 10, 15)
)

highchart() |>
  hc_chart(type = "bar") |>
  hc_title(text = "How do you feel about reading?") |>
  hc_xAxis(categories = survey$item) |>
  hc_yAxis(
    min = -100,
    max = 100,
    title = list(text = "Share of responses"),
    labels = list(
      formatter = JS("function () { return Math.abs(this.value) + '%'; }")
    )
  ) |>
  hc_plotOptions(series = list(stacking = "normal", borderWidth = 0)) |>
  hc_add_series(
    name = "Strongly disagree",
    data = -survey$strongly_disagree,
    color = "#96422f",
    legendIndex = 0
  ) |>
  hc_add_series(
    name = "Disagree",
    data = -survey$disagree,
    color = "#dc9b82",
    legendIndex = 1
  ) |>
  hc_add_series(
    name = "Strongly agree",
    data = survey$strongly_agree,
    color = "#22685d",
    legendIndex = 4
  ) |>
  hc_add_series(
    name = "Agree",
    data = survey$agree,
    color = "#76b5a4",
    legendIndex = 3
  ) |>
  hc_add_series(
    name = "Neutral",
    id = "neutral",
    data = survey$neutral / 2,
    color = "#c8c8c8",
    legendIndex = 2
  ) |>
  hc_add_series(
    name = "Neutral",
    linkedTo = "neutral",
    data = -survey$neutral / 2,
    color = "#c8c8c8"
  ) |>
  hc_tooltip(
    formatter = JS(
      "function () {
    const share = Math.abs(this.y) * (this.series.name === 'Neutral' ? 2 : 1);
    return this.category + '<br>' + this.series.name + ': ' + share + '%';
  }"
    )
  )
```

## Daily temperature range

Inspired by [Weather Radials](http://weather-radials.com/), each spoke shows one day in Santiago in 2025. Its ends mark the minimum and
maximum temperature, and its color reflects the daily mean. The monthly lines
in `highcharts_demo()` average those same daily means for each city.

```{r weather, echo=FALSE}
santiago <- subset(city_weather, city == "Santiago")

hchart(
  santiago,
  type = "columnrange",
  hcaes(x = date, low = temp_min, high = temp_max, color = temp_mean)
) |>
  hc_chart(polar = TRUE) |>
  hc_yAxis(
    title = list(text = NULL),
    labels = list(format = "{value} °C"),
    showFirstLabel = FALSE
  ) |>
  hc_xAxis(
    title = list(text = NULL),
    gridLineWidth = 0.5,
    labels = list(format = "{value:%b}")
  ) |>
  hc_tooltip(
    headerFormat = "<b>{point.x:%e %B %Y}</b><br>",
    pointFormat = "Min: {point.low} °C<br>Mean: {point.temp_mean} °C<br>Max: {point.high} °C"
  ) |>
  hc_title(text = "Daily temperature range in Santiago, 2025") |>
  hc_subtitle(text = "ERA5 reanalysis via Open-Meteo") |>
  hc_size(
    height = 600
  )
```

## Stars

Inspired by Nadieh Bremer's [block](http://bl.ocks.org/nbremer/eb0d1fd4118b731d069e2ff98dfadc47).
[Download the star sample (CSV)](data/stars.csv).

```{r stars, echo=FALSE}
stars <- read.csv("data/stars.csv")

colors <- c(
  "#FB1108",
  "#FD150B",
  "#FA7806",
  "#FBE426",
  "#FCFB8F",
  "#F3F5E7",
  "#C7E4EA",
  "#ABD6E6",
  "#9AD2E1"
)

stars$color <- highcharter::colorize(log(stars$temp), colors)

x <- c("Luminosity", "Temperature", "Distance", "Radius")
y <- sprintf("{point.%s:.2f}", c("lum", "temp", "distance", "radiussun"))

tltip <- tooltip_table(x, y)

hchart(
  stars,
  "scatter",
  hcaes(
    temp,
    lum,
    size = radiussun,
    color = color
  ),
  minSize = 2,
  maxSize = 20
) |>
  hc_chart(
    # backgroundColor = "black"
    backgroundColor = hex_to_rgba("#071426", 0.88),
    divBackgroundImage = "../stars-field.jpg"
  ) |>
  hc_xAxis(
    title = list(text = "Temperature", style = list(color = "#F2F6FF")),
    type = "logarithmic",
    gridLineWidth = 0,
    reversed = TRUE,
    labels = list(style = list(color = "#F2F6FF")),
    lineColor = "#A9B9D2"
  ) |>
  hc_yAxis(
    title = list(text = "Luminosity", style = list(color = "#F2F6FF")),
    type = "logarithmic",
    gridLineWidth = 0,
    labels = list(style = list(color = "#F2F6FF")),
    lineColor = "#A9B9D2"
  ) |>
  hc_title(
    style = list(color = "#F2F6FF"),
    text = "Our nearest Stars"
  ) |>
  hc_subtitle(
    style = list(color = "#DCE5EF"),
    text = "In a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram"
  ) |>
  hc_tooltip(
    useHTML = TRUE,
    headerFormat = "",
    pointFormat = tltip
  ) |>
  hc_size(
    height = 700
  )
```

## Volcanoes along the southern Andes

Eight volcanoes form a chain inland from the offshore boundary of the Nazca
and South American plates. Hover over a triangle to identify a volcano. The
GeoJSON contains the boundary as a line and the volcanoes as points, so the
two layers get separate legend entries. [Download the map layers](data/southern-andes.geojson).

```{r andes-volcanoes, echo=FALSE}
andes <- geojsonio::geojson_list(geojsonio::as.json(
  "data/southern-andes.geojson"
))

hcmap(
  "cl",
  name = "Chile",
  nullColor = "#e5eceb",
  enableMouseTracking = FALSE,
  showInLegend = FALSE
) |>
  hc_add_series(data = andes, name = c("Plate boundary", "Volcanoes")) |>
  hc_mapView(
    fitToGeometry = list(
      type = "MultiPoint",
      coordinates = list(c(-76, -42.5), c(-70.4, -35.7))
    )
  ) |>
  hc_plotOptions(
    mapline = list(color = "#265675", lineWidth = 3),
    mappoint = list(
      color = "#b34e30",
      marker = list(symbol = "triangle", radius = 5),
      dataLabels = list(
        filter = list(property = "name", operator = "==", value = "Villarrica")
      )
    )
  ) |>
  hc_legend(enabled = TRUE) |>
  hc_title(text = "Volcanoes along the southern Andes") |>
  hc_tooltip(headerFormat = "", pointFormat = "{point.name}")
```

Volcano locations come from the [Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program](https://volcano.si.edu/).
The boundary comes from Peter Bird’s [PB2002 model](https://doi.org/10.1029/2001GC000252),
converted to GeoJSON by [Hugo Ahlenius, Nordpil and contributors](https://github.com/fraxen/tectonicplates).

### Explore the global distribution

Switch from the regional view to the full Holocene catalogue. Each triangle
marks a volcano, including submarine features. Hover for its name, country,
landform and elevation. Toggle the plate boundaries in the legend to compare
the volcanic arcs around the Pacific with volcanoes in plate interiors.

```{r global-volcanoes, echo=FALSE}
volcanoes <- read.csv("data/holocene-volcanoes.csv.gz")
plates <- jsonlite::read_json("data/plate-boundaries.geojson.gz")

hcmap(
  "custom/world.topo.json",
  name = "Land",
  showInLegend = FALSE,
  nullColor = "rgba(92,126,118,0.20)",
  borderWidth = 0.3,
  enableMouseTracking = FALSE
) |>
  hc_add_series(
    type = "mapline",
    name = "Plate boundaries",
    data = lapply(plates$features, function(f) list(geometry = f$geometry)),
    color = "#547682",
    lineWidth = 1.2,
    enableMouseTracking = FALSE
  ) |>
  hc_add_series(
    volcanoes,
    "mappoint",
    hcaes(name = name, lon = lon, lat = lat),
    name = "Holocene volcanoes",
    color = "rgba(175,68,40,0.76)",
    marker = list(symbol = "triangle", radius = 3),
    dataLabels = list(enabled = FALSE),
    turboThreshold = 0
  ) |>
  hc_title(text = "Volcanoes and plate boundaries") |>
  hc_subtitle(
    text = "1,215 Holocene volcanoes · Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program"
  ) |>
  hc_legend(enabled = TRUE) |>
  hc_mapNavigation(enabled = TRUE, enableMouseWheelZoom = FALSE) |>
  hc_tooltip(
    headerFormat = "",
    pointFormat = "<b>{point.name}</b> · {point.country}<br>{point.landform}<br>Elevation: {point.elevation:,.0f} m"
  ) |>
  hc_caption(
    text = "Volcanoes: Smithsonian GVP · Boundaries: Peter Bird (PB2002), via Nordpil."
  )
```

## South Atlantic wind field

On 27 March 2004, Hurricane Catarina approached southern Brazil. This snapshot
shows ERA5 wind at 10 m at 18:00 UTC. Each arrow points downwind and its color
gives the speed. Sampling the 0.25° reanalysis every 0.75° keeps the circulation
legible at this scale. Hover over an arrow for its speed and bearing.
[Copernicus ERA5](https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.adbb2d47) ·
[NASA satellite image of Catarina](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/rare-south-atlantic-tropical-cyclone-12939/).

```{r catarina, echo=FALSE}
wind <- read.csv(system.file(
  "extdata",
  "catarina-wind.csv",
  package = "highcharter"
))
wind$speed <- sqrt(wind$u^2 + wind$v^2)
wind$bearing <- (atan2(wind$u, wind$v) * 180 / pi + 360) %% 360

# Draw each arrow in local east/north coordinates, then convert to longitude/latitude.
arrows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(wind)), function(i) {
  cell <- wind[i, ]
  angle <- cell$bearing * pi / 180
  along <- c(-0.24, 0.24, 0.08, 0.24, 0.08)
  across <- c(0, 0, -0.09, 0, 0.09)
  east <- along * sin(angle) + across * cos(angle)
  north <- along * cos(angle) - across * sin(angle)
  coordinates <- Map(
    c,
    cell$lon + east / cos(cell$lat * pi / 180),
    cell$lat + north
  )
  list(
    value = cell$speed,
    bearing = cell$bearing,
    lon = cell$lon,
    lat = cell$lat,
    geometry = list(type = "LineString", coordinates = coordinates)
  )
})

hcmap(
  "custom/world.topo.json",
  nullColor = "#f0eee8",
  borderColor = "#a8b1af",
  showInLegend = FALSE,
  enableMouseTracking = FALSE
) |>
  hc_chart(plotBackgroundColor = "#eaf3f6") |>
  hc_mapView(
    projection = list(name = "WebMercator"),
    padding = 0,
    fitToGeometry = list(
      type = "MultiPoint",
      coordinates = list(c(-56, -33.5), c(-40.5, -22.75))
    )
  ) |>
  hc_add_series(
    type = "mapline",
    name = "10 m wind",
    data = arrows,
    colorKey = "value",
    lineWidth = 2,
    tooltip = list(
      pointFormat = "{point.lat:.1f}°, {point.lon:.1f}° · {point.value:.1f} m/s towards {point.bearing:.0f}°"
    )
  ) |>
  hc_colorAxis(
    min = 0,
    max = 15,
    tickPositions = c(0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15),
    stops = color_stops(colors = c("#497991", "#137b78", "#c87b21", "#a63742"))
  ) |>
  hc_legend(
    layout = "horizontal",
    align = "center",
    title = list(text = "Wind speed (m/s)")
  ) |>
  hc_add_series(
    type = "mappoint",
    name = "Coastal cities",
    showInLegend = FALSE,
    color = "#45434a",
    marker = list(radius = 2),
    data = list(
      list(name = "Florianópolis", lon = -48.55, lat = -27.60),
      list(name = "Porto Alegre", lon = -51.23, lat = -30.03)
    ),
    dataLabels = list(
      enabled = TRUE,
      format = "{point.name}",
      align = "right",
      style = list(fontSize = "10px", fontWeight = "normal")
    )
  ) |>
  hc_caption(
    text = "Wind: Copernicus Climate Change Service (ERA5), sampled at 0.75°."
  ) |>
  hc_title(text = "Catarina off the coast of Brazil") |>
  hc_subtitle(text = "Surface wind · 27 March 2004, 18:00 UTC") |>
  hc_size(height = 500)
```

## Icons and pictograms

### Icons as markers

The [fontawesome package](https://rstudio.github.io/fontawesome/) provides SVG
icons that can be used in markers and tooltips. These are the original R and
Python examples, with the same data and colors. Embedding the SVG directly keeps
the icons sharp and avoids an intermediate PNG file.

```{r svg-markers, echo=FALSE}
set.seed(123)
df <- data.frame(
  a = round(rnorm(10), 2),
  b = round(rnorm(10), 2)
)

fa_to_data_uri <- function(name, fill, width = 22) {
  size <- paste0(width, "px")
  icon <- fontawesome::fa(name, fill = fill, width = size, height = size)
  svg <- as.character(icon)
  # Standalone images need an XML namespace and intrinsic pixel dimensions.
  svg <- sub(
    "<svg",
    sprintf(
      '<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="%s" height="%s"',
      width,
      width
    ),
    svg,
    fixed = TRUE
  )
  svg <- sub(
    'preserveAspectRatio="none"',
    'preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"',
    svg,
    fixed = TRUE
  )
  paste0(
    "data:image/svg+xml,",
    utils::URLencode(svg, reserved = TRUE)
  )
}

# Reuse the same colors in markers, series and tooltips.
rcol <- "#4C83B6"
pcol <- "#3CAB48"
rproj <- fa_to_data_uri("r-project", fill = rcol)
pthon <- fa_to_data_uri("python", fill = pcol)

highchart() |>
  hc_title(text = "Font Awesome icons") |>
  hc_add_series(
    df,
    "scatter",
    hcaes(a, b),
    name = "R icons",
    color = rcol,
    marker = list(symbol = paste0("url(", rproj, ")")),
    icon = as.character(fontawesome::fa(
      "r-project",
      fill = rcol,
      height = "15px",
      vertical_align = "middle"
    ))
  ) |>
  hc_add_series(
    df,
    "scatter",
    hcaes(b, a),
    name = "Python icons",
    color = pcol,
    marker = list(symbol = paste0("url(", pthon, ")")),
    icon = as.character(fontawesome::fa(
      "python",
      fill = pcol,
      height = "15px",
      vertical_align = "middle"
    ))
  ) |>
  hc_tooltip(
    useHTML = TRUE,
    pointFormat = paste0(
      "<b>",
      "{series.options.icon} ",
      "[{point.x}, {point.y}]",
      "</b>"
    )
  )
```

### Count with pictograms

This example, inspired by [waffle](https://github.com/hrbrmstr/waffle), uses the
original food categories, counts and colors. Each symbol represents one unit.

```{r item-icons, echo=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

df2 <- tibble(
  type = c("fruit", "samminch", "pizza"),
  amount = c(46, 54, 80),
  faico = c("apple", "bread-slice", "pizza-slice"),
  col = c("#d35400", "#907E4D", "#F89101")
) |>
  mutate(
    uri = map2_chr(faico, col, ~ fa_to_data_uri(.x, fill = .y)),
    marker = map(uri, ~ list(symbol = paste0("url(", .x, ")")))
  )

hchart(
  df2,
  "item",
  hcaes(name = type, y = amount),
  name = "What I eat",
  showInLegend = TRUE
) |>
  hc_legend(labelFormat = "{name} <span style='opacity: 0.4'>{y}</span>") |>
  hc_colors(pull(df2, col))
```
